title: MB1-01552
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: These are the reasons for decision regarding the claim for refugee protection filed by XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Guinea. He is alleging a well-founded fear of persecution in Guinea by reason of his membership in a particular social group, the family. He is also claiming protection as a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), because he would be subjected to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

According to his Personal Information Form (PIF),1 submitted in support of his claim for refugee protection, the claimant was born on April 28, 1986. He is single and, after his studies, he worked as a merchant from 2008 to 2010. He maintained that he is wanted by the military authorities in his country.

In his narrative, the claimant states that he took over the family business. The first problem that he encountered was that the authorities wanted him to XXXX XXXX XXXX des forces guinéennes [Guinean military XXXX] to XXXX XXXX. The second problem mentioned is that he is a Malinke and, according to his narrative, the Fulani have a monopoly over the public market.
He stated that there were two noteworthy candidates from the country's two main ethnic groups for the presidential election, which divided support in Guinea.

The claimant pointed out that there are Fulani in his neighbourhood who XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that some people have suffered from it. The XXXX XXXX was after the claimant because he had been arrested as a result of the claimant's denunciation. He decided to leave the country.

The claimant stated that he boarded a boat and left his country on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, without knowing where he was headed. He stated that he spent many months on the boat. When he arrived in a strange country, he boarded a white minivan and travelled a long distance. He spoke to a woman who told him that he was now in Canada. The claimant then asked to be taken to the Guinean community.

As previously mentioned, the claimant left his country by boat on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, and arrived in Canada at an unknown port. He declared to the Canadian authorities that he wanted to claim refugee protection on February 28, 2011. As for his fear of returning, the claimant stated that he fears the army and the police authorities who are working for the XXXX XXXX whom the claimant denounced.

The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity because some documents, including his national identity card, were seized by the immigration authorities in Canada. The claimant also submitted his driver's licence and diplomas in a bundle.

First, the refugee protection claimant is basing his claim on the ground that he is a "Convention refugee" because he claims to have a well-founded fear of being persecuted by certain authorities by reason of his membership in a particular social group, namely the family and his ethnic group, the Malinke.
Having heard the testimony and analyzed all of the evidence, the panel concludes that there is no basis for allowing the claim, given that the refugee protection claimant is not credible.

At the start of the hearing, the panel asked for some clarifications. He stated that he left his country on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, and that his problems dated back to XXXX XXXX of the same year. He fears the person whom he denounced, the person who allegedly XXXX XXXX XXXX. When asked to explain when he decided to leave the country, the claimant gave surprising answers. He stated that he did not make the decision to leave. He added that he had problems and that he was running his business. Then he added the issue of XXXX and his ethnic problem and concluded that he made the decision to leave on XXXX XXXX, 2010. He did not have a specific destination, but simply wanted to save his life.

The claimant expounded at length on his problem, which is that he did not want to participate XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a team that was allegedly affiliated with the army in his country. He added that he never liked the army and that furthermore, military service is not mandatory. In fact, if military service is not mandatory, the claimant is not obliged to participate and even less XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX that is allegedly affiliated with the army. It appears that he was offered a contract to join that XXXX XXXX. He associates the XXXX XXXX with his country's army. The claimant stated that he was pressured to XXXX XXXX XXXX. However, he never joined that organization. The panel can only reject the claimant's explanations regarding his involvement and his integration in the Guinean army, because he was not a member of that XXXX XXXX and, consequently, he was not integrated into the Guinean forces, which, furthermore, is not mandatory.

Another problem has to do with the claimant's denunciation of a Fulani XXXX XXXX. Allegedly, the claimant denounced the situation, and this merchant was arrested. When the claimant was confronted with this situation, to find out whether he had filed a complaint with the authorities, the claimant replied that he had not because it was not relevant. However, a few seconds earlier, he indicated that he had reported the situation of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that the latter had been convicted. The panel cannot understand the claimant's reasoning; if he denounced this XXXX XXXX XXXX, the fact is that the authorities took action against this XXXX XXXX following the claimant's denunciation and that, furthermore, if the claimant had actually been roughed up by this XXXX XXXX, he could have once again denounced him to the authorities. The claimant defended himself by stating that the XXXX XXXX was very influential in the community. Despite the claimant's assertion, we understand that, as a result of the claimant's first denunciation, the XXXX XXXX was arrested; therefore, if there were any other problems with this person, he could have reported him again. The panel does not understand the claimant's reasoning on this subject.

A major addition was made at the hearing. The claimant stated that his mother was called upon twice to appear at the police station in XXXX 2011. This incident is not mentioned in his narrative, which was submitted in the immigration documents that the claimant completed. We were not given a satisfactory explanation for this and are of the opinion that the claimant tried to exaggerate his story.

The panel also noted a particular sentence in the claimant's narrative. When he arrived in Canada, he allegedly asked someone to take him to the Guinean community. If, as he claims, he fears various people from the Guinean community, the panel finds it peculiar, to say the least, that he would want to meet people from his community, some of whom could be from another ethnic group and could, consequently, hold it against him. He stated that he simply wanted to find housing. The panel can only reject this unsatisfactory explanation and, in the circumstances, we are of the opinion that his testimony contradicts his subjective fear.

The panel also questioned the claimant about the last presidential election. The claimant pointed out that the president is Alpha Condé. When asked to explain the President's ethnic origin, he replied that he is Malinke, like himself, and that the opponent is Fulani. If the claimant fears for his safety because of his ethnic background and the problems that he allegedly had with a XXXX XXXX, the fact is that the leaders of his country are from the same ethnic group as he is, and that Mr. Condé obtained 52.5% of the votes, according to the documentary evidence on file.2
The panel briefly discussed an internal flight alternative in the city of Kankan, and he mentioned that he could not go there.

We will not address the claimant's itinerary for his trip to Canada. We have no corroborating documentation to support the claimant's allegations that he left his country on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, and even less regarding his itinerary at sea. According to what we have been told, he was at sea for many months and stayed hidden in a cabin. Furthermore, if it is true that he arrived at a Canadian port, it appears that the claimant did not encounter any Canadian authorities on the docks and was able to cross the border at the port that he had arrived at. The panel has serious doubts about this portion of the claimant's narrative.

In light of the testimony given and the evidence on file, the refugee protection claimant did not discharge his burden of establishing that he has a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of his particular social group, namely, the family and the ethnic group that he belongs to in Guinea.

Second, since the panel has rejected his claim for refugee protection on the basis that he is not credible, the same outcome must be reserved for the ground of a risk to his life and a risk of cruel and unusual treatment.

Lastly, the claimant based his claim for refugee protection on the ground that he could be subjected to a danger of torture, as per Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture. Given the evidence submitted, the claimant confirmed that military service is not mandatory in his country and that he obtained identity documents in 2009, prior to the alleged date of his departure. Furthermore, we note that the claimant, who filed a complaint with the police authorities, received at least some satisfaction, considering that the person whom he had denounced was arrested by those same authorities. Consequently, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant is not wanted by the police authorities in his country.

The refugee protection claimant did not discharge his burden of establishing that he has a well-founded fear of persecution in Guinea, his country of nationality. Consequently, for the aforementioned reasons, the panel determines that the refugee protection claimant, XXXX XXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of IRPA or a "person in need of protection" pursuant to paragraphs 97(1)(a) and (b) of the IRPA, mentioned previously.

Consequently, the panel rejects the claim for refugee protection Michel Jobin Me Michel Jobin January 9, 2013 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Exhibit P-1: Personal Information Form (PIF). 2 Exhibit A-1: Index of the National Documentation Package on Guinea, June 15, 2012, Tab 2.1: United States.
